title: Americans on AI

contributors.display_name: NORC at the University of Chicago

methodology_notes:
Americans on AI is a tracking study of U.S. adults' views on artificial
intelligence. The pilot wave (June 12-18, 2026) was fielded on the Prolific
online panel (nonprobability) and weighted by raking to American Community
Survey 2024 1-year benchmarks for sex, age, and race/ethnicity. Subsequent
waves are fielded by NORC at the University of Chicago on the probability-based
AmeriSpeak Panel; NORC supplies the final weights, raked to March Current Population
Survey benchmarks over age, sex, census division, race/ethnicity, and
education. Party identification is never a weighting target, so shifts in
party composition remain visible across waves; note that the pilot measures
party as unleaned self-report while NORC waves fold leaners into the parties.
All published percentages are weighted and use the full sample as the base,
with "Not sure" and "No answer" shown as categories where applicable; the
forced-response pilot has no "No answer" category. Race/ethnicity subgroups
are published from the June 2026 NORC wave onward. Percentages are reported
to two decimal places and may not sum to exactly 100 due to rounding.

dimensions.text: Thinking about AI's growing role in society, which of these options comes closest to how you feel, even if none are exactly right?

codes.label: None of these are close to how I feel

questions.notes: Asked as a forced choice between the two statements in the pilot wave; from the June 2026 NORC wave a third presented option ("Neither of these are close to how I feel") was added. Distributions and the agency net are not directly comparable across that change.

dimensions.text: Again, thinking about AI, which statement comes closer to your view, even if neither is exactly right?

codes.label: People like me can shape how much AI is part of our lives
AI is coming into our lives whether we want it or not
Neither of these are close to how I feel

questions.stem: Thinking about your local community, how much are you seeing each of the following changes because of AI?

dimensions.text: People are saving time on everyday tasks
People are pressured to do more, faster
People are losing connections to others
People are struggling to tell what's real from what's fake
People are getting better health care

questions.stem: Thinking about families in America today, how is AI affecting each of the following?
When it comes to each of the following issues, is the government doing too much, too little, or about the right amount in response?

dimensions.text: AI's effects on children and young people
AI's environmental footprint, including from data centers
AI's effects on workers and jobs

questions.stem: Thinking about the next 20 years, how likely is each of the following to happen?

dimensions.text: AI becoming smarter than humans at most tasks
AI systems behaving in ways their developers did not intend
AI making major scientific and medical breakthroughs
AI being used to create weapons of mass destruction

codes.label: Not at all likely to happen

nets.label: Unlikely or not at all likely (sum)

waves.label: Pilot — June 12–18, 2026

weighting.notes: Raked to American Community Survey 2024 1-year sex, age, and race/ethnicity margins. Party identification is not a weighting target. Design effect 1.097; effective sample size 1640.

waves.notes: Nonprobability pilot wave fielded on Prolific with forced-response items, so no item nonresponse appears. Party identification is respondent self-report (Democrat/Independent/Republican) without leaner allocation, unlike later waves where leaners fold into the parties. Race/ethnicity subgroups are not published for this wave: the panel's race categories cannot separate Hispanic ethnicity.

waves.label: June 2026

weighting.notes: NORC-supplied final client weight (WEIGHT_ATH), raked to March Current Population Survey benchmarks over age, sex, census division, race/ethnicity, and education. Standard errors use Taylor linearization over NORC's strata and PSUs. Party identification is not itself a weighting target, though a second round of raking calibrates the weights to 2024 presidential vote choice. Black respondents were oversampled by design; weights adjust to national benchmarks. Design effect 2.125; effective sample size 854.

waves.notes: Fielded by NORC on the probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel in mixed mode (about 90% web, 10% phone). Item nonresponse is permitted from this wave: "No answer" categories absorb skipped and refused items. Party identification uses NORC's three-way party coding with leaners folded into the parties.

waves.label: July (W1) 2026

weighting.notes: NORC-supplied final client weight (delivered as WEIGHT_VC this wave), raked to March Current Population Survey benchmarks over age, sex, census division, race/ethnicity, and education. Standard errors use Taylor linearization over NORC's strata and PSUs. Party identification is not itself a weighting target, though a second round of raking calibrates the weights to 2024 presidential vote choice. No oversamples this wave. Design effect 1.955; effective sample size 540.

waves.notes: Fielded by NORC on the probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel in mixed mode (about 94% web, 6% phone). Item nonresponse is permitted: "No answer" categories absorb skipped and refused items. Party identification uses NORC's three-way party coding with leaners folded into the parties. No oversamples this wave, so subgroup bases follow population shares; the Black, non-Hispanic base is small (n=92) and its margins of error widen accordingly.

waves.label: July (W2) 2026

weighting.notes: NORC-supplied final client weight (delivered as WEIGHT_VC this wave), raked to March Current Population Survey benchmarks over age, sex, census division, race/ethnicity, and education. Standard errors use Taylor linearization over NORC's strata and PSUs. Party identification is not itself a weighting target, though a second round of raking calibrates the weights to 2024 presidential vote choice. The delivery carried a second weight (WEIGHT_ATH) on the same strata and PSUs but with a different calibration; the one used here continues the weighting construct of the earlier waves. Design effect 1.851; effective sample size 981.

waves.notes: Fielded by NORC on the probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel in mixed mode (about 96% web, 4% phone). Item nonresponse is permitted: "No answer" categories absorb skipped and refused items. Party identification uses NORC's three-way party coding with leaners folded into the parties. Black, non-Hispanic and Hispanic respondents were oversampled by design, improving those subgroup margins; the weights restore population proportions.
